correctness.rationale: A selected spine vertex observes both spine vertices and at least one nonspine vertex on each page; each missing page vertex is then forced. Without a selected spine vertex, a hit page is fully observed by the initial step and supplies whichever spine vertex is not yet observed. If exactly one page was missed, each spine vertex can force its neighbor there. For two or more missed pages both spine vertices have at least two unobserved neighbors there and no observed nonspine vertex is adjacent to a missed page, so none can be entered. The empty set fails. With q=2x+x², the disjoint cases count as q(1+x)^(2n), q^n and n q^(n−1). At x=1 and in degree one this gives the claimed total and minimum layers. At n=2 the criterion is exactly nonemptiness; at n=1 the formula would add a spurious constant, so the exclusion is necessary and C₄ has all nonempty sets. An independent replay exhausted 349,504 subsets for 2≤n≤8 and matched the classification, all coefficients, total counts and singleton counts. The case analysis, not the finite replay, proves the result for all n.
residual_risks: The replay checks graphs only through order 18; no formal certificate is inferred.

evidence: Brimkov et al.'s generic fort criterion applies: the union of the nonspine vertices on two untouched pages is a fort whose closed neighborhood is missed when S avoids those pages and the spine. The cited decomposition passages concern disjoint union, join and vertex identification, not direct enumeration for pages sharing an edge.
The Dorbec et al. abstract is about minimum power-domination numbers for product classes, not all-cardinality enumeration for this family. The cited Benson et al. paper was not read in full.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The fort criterion explains the obstruction but still requires a graph-specific computation and a sufficiency argument to obtain the frozen classification. The exact prior indexed result, not a generic algorithm, is decisive.
